title: Tracing platform
brief: Store distributed traces for 500 teams and make an exemplar link open the useful trace during an incident. Decide what to sample before storage, handle late spans, and keep query traffic from overwhelming ingestion. Keeping all errors is a policy goal with a failure boundary, not a magic property of sampling.

clarify.a: About 10,000 traces/s, 20 spans/trace and 500 bytes/span before compression. A tail decision window of 30 seconds requires at least 3 GB of raw buffering before overhead and redundancy (approx.).

No. Plan a representative 10% baseline and prioritize error and slow traces subject to a hard byte budget. The modeled storage load is the 10% baseline. An error-heavy incident can exceed it, so reserve capacity or explicitly shed lower-priority samples.

Route a trace id to one decision group, persist decisions for a bounded late-span window and append late spans consistently where possible. Mark incomplete traces. Collector loss or upstream sampling can still remove evidence.

Retained 100 MB blocks and small trace-id reads after sampling. Tail assembly, outcome selection and full attribute searches are worked obligations; placing the Traces observer does not implement a tracing platform.

notes: Raw incoming spans are about 100 MB/s; 10% retention gives about 10 MB/s before compression. One catalog batch is 100 MB, so 0.1 retained blocks/s is the planning rate (approx.).
Seven days at that retained rate is about 6.048 TB, before indexes, replication and an error reserve (approx.).
The block queue is after sampling. It does not protect spans not yet selected. Durable collector spooling or an explicit loss budget is a separate decision.

The current sim applies a global request mix. All source paths share a real authenticated front door. workloadPlan records source-specific rates for a later engine; it is descriptive and does not affect this score.

numbers.label: Thirty-second raw tail buffer
numbers.how: 100 MB/s × 30 seconds, before metadata and redundancy (approx.).

hints: Does the sampling decision need to know whether the request eventually failed?
Head sampling saves network earlier but cannot see future errors. Tail sampling receives and buffers spans before choosing. Keep all spans of a trace on one decision group.

After the sampler, durable block staging and workers write object storage. Trace-id lookups use a cache. Budget and test collector memory, late decisions, raw ingest and error-priority overflow separately.

editorial.summary: Collectors propagate trace context, redact sensitive attributes and group spans by trace id. Choose head sampling when early bandwidth control dominates; choose tail selection for outcome-based retention with bounded memory, a late-span policy and explicit overflow. Blocks in object storage and a trace-id index serve retrieval. The reference begins after the collector's sampling decision, so its traffic score is not evidence that the sampler can handle the raw stream.

designs.name: Retained blocks with cached trace lookups
designs.why: The shared API accepts already selected blocks into a durable queue. Builders publish immutable blocks and a derived trace-id lookup structure. Small trace-id lookups read cached object/index data. The collector stays a distinct upstream protocol obligation, rather than an observer falsely placed on the request path. Source-specific roles are recorded for later engine support.

tradeoffs: Head sampling can discard the trace before an error occurs. Select consistently by trace id so services do not independently retain fragments.
Tail sampling can prioritize observed errors but must receive the raw stream and wait. A 30-second window needs about 3 GB raw state here; process overhead, replicas and long traces add more.
At 100 MB/s raw, a hard 10 MB/s storage budget cannot keep every trace if errors dominate. Reserve capacity and prioritize, or declare a loss policy. Monitor dropped and incomplete traces.
A trace-id index is small compared with indexing every attribute. Arbitrary attribute search needs additional indexes or bounded block scans with its own budget.

Keep complete request metrics for SLI denominators. Outcome-biased retained traces cannot directly measure the population error rate. Exemplars link selected observations without making trace ids metric labels.
editorial.realWorld: This example has about 200,000 spans/s before sampling. Ten percent baseline storage is about 864 GB/day before compression; actual retention rises when error-priority traces exceed the baseline. Collector buffering and query scans need separate measurements (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A collector has seen only successful spans when its tail decision timer expires. A late error span arrives afterwards. What is your policy and how is its loss measured?
correctness.discussion: Keep a bounded decision cache keyed by tenant and trace id so late spans follow an explicit prior decision or a documented promotion rule. Mark incompleteness, count late and dropped spans, and bound memory and decision lifetime. A head sampler upstream may already have removed evidence. Collector restart needs durable spooling and replay if the loss budget demands it. No tail policy guarantees all errors across unobserved or discarded spans. Request metrics must count the whole population independently.

fields.label: Tail capacity
options: Receive raw spans and budget decision state before retention
fields.explanation: Outcome selection needs the data before it can choose what to discard.

fields.label: Error-rate source
options: Errors divided by retained tail-sampled traces
fields.explanation: Tail retention is biased by outcome; it does not supply an unbiased denominator.

correctness.limits: The score starts after sampling and does not validate trace assembly, sampling bias, context propagation or collector recovery.
